title: Implicit interest rates in medieval bills of exchange, 14 currency pairs (28 directions), Datini archive, 1380–1411
source: A. R. Bell, C. Brooks and T. K. Moore, 'Cambium non est mutuum: exchange and interest rates in medieval Europe', Economic History Review 70(2): 373–396 (2017), Tables 4 and 5 (accepted manuscript, CentAUR 57199)
series: Table 4 'Implicit interest rates from the Datini archive, 1380-1411': CityFrom, CityTo, Term (days, the sum of the usances there and back), Match (days), Number (observations), Spread, Simple APR, Compounded APR; Table 5 'Risk and return': Negative return, Spread STDEV, APR compounded STDEV (adjusted for the number of operations a year), Sharpe ratio (benchmark 8%). Columns here: city_from, city_to, term_days, match_days, observations, spread_pct, simple_apr_pct, compounded_apr_pct, negative_return_pct, spread_sd_pct, compounded_apr_sd_pct, sharpe
license: Numbers transcribed from two published tables for teaching and comment, with attribution; the accepted manuscript is deposited in CentAUR (University of Reading) under its end-user agreement.
notes: Transcribed from the text layer of the PDF (pdftotext -layout; SHA-256 5ca0d1dd0d4951de338eab3c913ef4446bd331555dbe36c67c58d1a9204330bd) by a script that also checked that the two tables list the same 28 pairs in the same order with the same mean spread and compounded APR. Percentages are stored as numbers (4.40 = 4.40%). Checks (checks/check_ch10.py): the simple APR equals spread × 365 / term within 0.05 percentage points in 27 rows; Bruges→Paris is printed as 11.55% but 1.33% × 365/46 = 10.55%, and its compounded APR (11.53%) is below the printed simple APR, so 11.55 is taken to be a misprint and the row is kept as printed. The Sharpe ratio equals (compounded APR − 8)/adjusted SD in every row. The compounded APR is the mean of the annualized returns of the individual matched transactions, so it is not equal to (1 + mean spread)^(365/term) − 1; the chapter annualizes the mean spread itself (simple) and quotes the compounded figures as printed. The text of the paper gives the Florence→Venice share of negative returns as 9.4% (81 of 832), but 81/832 = 9.74%, as in Table 5. The text of the paper (p. 20) gives the Genoa–London mean spread and standard deviation as 6.82% and 3.56%, while Table 5 gives 6.85% and 3.87% for Genoa→London; the chapter uses Table 5. Either way the standard deviation is more than half the mean.
